flawed_step: Regularity and edge-transitivity do not force an automorphism to interchange the two bipartition classes; semisymmetric graphs are counterexamples.
counterexample: Let coordinates range over {0,1,2}. Form a bipartite graph with 27 point-vertices P(a,b,c) and 27 axis-line vertices X(b,c), Y(a,c), Z(a,b). Join P(a,b,c) to exactly X(b,c), Y(a,c), and Z(a,b). Thus every vertex has degree 3. The graph is edge-transitive: permutations of the three coordinate directions, together with independent permutations of the three values in each coordinate, act transitively on incident point-line pairs. It is not vertex-transitive. To see this intrinsically, within either bipartition class join two vertices when they have a common neighbor in the original graph. On the point side this is Hamming graph H(3,3); two nonadjacent points have either 0 or 2 common neighbors, never exactly 1. On the line side, X(0,0) and Y(0,1) are nonadjacent but have exactly one common neighbor, namely Z(0,0). Hence the two derived graphs are not isomorphic, so no automorphism can interchange the bipartition classes. Therefore point-vertices and line-vertices lie in different automorphism orbits.
assessment_summary: The 54-vertex cubic incidence graph of the 3×3×3 grid satisfies every hypothesis but is not vertex-transitive.
